scope: Round 2 re-grade of full-r2.json (33 genres): (1) every id in grade-1..4 re-read fresh; (2) every artist recording; (3) every study prompt, script-checked against its own card; (4) new reggaeton artist El General in full. Description/debatable are graded against the genre-level sources list, as in round 1.

items.claim: Kind of Blue (1959), planned around Bill Evans's piano style by two players who knew George Russell's ideas about modes
items.note: The round-1 fix reads as if Davis and Evans did the planning. The section says only, passively, that 'the music had been planned around Evans's piano style' and, separately, that both knew Russell's modal ideas.

fix.text: Kind of Blue (1959), whose music was planned around Bill Evans's piano style, is what some consider his greatest album; both Davis and Evans knew George Russell's ideas about modal jazz.

sources.section: 1957–1963: Collaborations with Gil Evans and Kind of Blue

items.claim: one writer calls it 'a construct' for many related musics, and Duke Ellington called his own work American Music rather than jazz
items.note: Now accurate to the corpus, but neither fact is in a cited section: Gabbard's 'jazz is a construct' is in Jazz 'Etymology and definition'; Ellington's 'American Music, rather than jazz' is in 'The influence of Duke Ellington'. Improvisation only says jazz is 'considered difficult to define'. Text can stay; add the two sources.

fix.text: Jazz is famously hard to define: one writer calls it 'a construct' for many related musics, and Duke Ellington called his own work American Music rather than jazz.

items.claim: Thomas Dorsey is often credited with creating it, though he more accurately spread a movement
items.cited: Gospel music Infobox; intro; Gospel goes to mainstream (genre sources)
items.note: 17th century, 1874 and 1930 are now supported. The Dorsey clause is still uncited: it comes from Thomas A. Dorsey intro ('often credited with creating it, Dorsey more accurately spawned a movement that popularized gospel blues'), which the card's sources don't include.

fix.text: There is no clean founding date: its roots are traced to the early 17th century, the term 'gospel song' first appeared in print in 1874, and 1930 is said to be the year traditional Black gospel began; Thomas Dorsey is often credited with creating it, though he more accurately started a movement that popularised gospel blues.

items.claim: it is now largely linked with white Americans, which has been put down to record labels segregating the music industry from the 1920s
items.cited: Country music Infobox; intro; Origins (genre sources)
items.note: Wording now matches the corpus but the only source is 'Race in modern country music' ('attributed to the efforts to segregate the music industry by record labels, beginning in the 1920s'), which is not among the card's sources. Add it.

fix.text: Its roots are both African and European, yet it is now largely linked with white Americans, which has been put down to record labels segregating the music industry from the 1920s.

items.note: Corpus gives death 25 August 2026. Supported by the corpus; still needs a live-source check before publish (after the grader's knowledge).

items.claim: Pete Seeger was a New York singer, banjo player and activist
items.cited: Folk revival Major figures; Pete Seeger intro
items.note: Banjo is now supported (Major figures: How to Play the Five-String Banjo). 'New York' is not in either cited section; it is only in Pete Seeger Infobox (birth place New York City), which isn't cited. Add the Infobox source.

fix.text: Pete Seeger was a New York-born singer, banjo player and activist, a fixture of 1940s radio and a member of The Weavers, who became a leading protest singer in the 1960s.

items.claim: some dictionaries treat the terms as the same
items.cited: Rock music Infobox; intro; Characteristics (genre sources)
items.note: The blanket-term half is in Characteristics. The dictionaries half is still only in Rock and roll 'Etymology' ('defined as such in some dictionaries'), which the card doesn't cite. Text fine; add the source.

fix.text: Where rock and roll ends and rock begins is blurry: some dictionaries treat the terms as the same, and in recent years 'rock' has even been used as a blanket term for pop, soul and hip-hop.

items.claim: though blues rock and psychedelic bands often stretched them into long improvised jams
items.note: Blues rock section: 'Blues rock bands often emulated jazz, playing long, involved improvisations'. It says nothing of psychedelic bands doing so (only that Cream and Hendrix moved into psychedelia). Drop 'psychedelic'.

fix.text: Mostly verse-chorus songs, though blues rock bands often stretched them into long, jazz-like improvisations.

items.claim: it grew up in several places at once ... Brisbane, where the Saints' Ed Kuepper said they'd been doing this sort of thing for years before hearing the Ramones
items.cited: Punk rock Infobox; intro; Outlook; Musical and lyrical elements; New York City; United Kingdom (genre sources)
items.note: The garage-band naming and the four scenes are in the intro. The Kuepper recollection is accurate but only in Punk rock 'Australia', which the card doesn't cite.

fix.text: The name came before the sound, since critics first used 'punk rock' for 1960s garage bands; and it grew up in several places at once: New York, Ohio, London and Brisbane, where the Saints' Ed Kuepper said they'd been doing this sort of thing for years before hearing the Ramones.

items.claim: The male American punk look ... harked back to 1950s greasers, later with ripped jeans and Doc Martens
items.cited: Punk rock Visual and other elements
items.note: Minor: the section says 'in addition to the T-shirt and leather jackets they wore ripped jeans and boots, typically Doc Martens'. It doesn't say these came later.

fix.text: A look to shock: The male American punk look of T-shirt, motorcycle jacket and jeans harked back to 1950s greasers, worn with ripped jeans and boots, typically Doc Martens. Women in punk tore up rock's old female roles, from Siouxsie Sioux's bondage gear to Patti Smith's androgyny.

items.claim: AllMusic's Bruce Eder called Sam Cooke 'the inventor of soul music'
items.cited: Soul music Infobox; intro; Origins; 1960s (genre sources)
items.note: Ray Charles (Origins) and Guralnick (1960s) are supported. The Eder quote is still only in Sam Cooke 'Legacy', which the card doesn't cite.

fix.text: Who started soul is argued over: Ray Charles is often cited as popularising it, AllMusic's Bruce Eder called Sam Cooke 'the inventor of soul music', and Peter Guralnick dates its start to Solomon Burke's 1961 'Just Out of Reach'.

items.claim: stayed popular in Italy and much of Europe through the 1980s
items.note: The 'every decade' stretch is fixed, but the intro says disco 'remained popular in Italy and some European countries throughout the 1980s'. 'Much of Europe' is stronger than 'some European countries'.

fix.text: Whether disco 'died' is debatable: it fell sharply in the US after Disco Demolition Night in July 1979, but stayed popular in Italy and some other European countries through the 1980s and has had several revivals since the 1990s.

items.claim: DJs ... began reworking disco records, adding drum machines, to give them a more mechanical beat. From there it spread to New York, London and Ibiza
items.cited: House music intro; Characteristics; Influences and precursors; 1980s; UK (genre sources)
items.note: 'Harder' is gone (fixed). Two small issues remain: (1) the drum-machine part is hedged in the source ('The constant bass drum in house music may have arisen from DJs experimenting with adding drum machines'), but the card states it as fact; (2) Ibiza is only in House music 'Ibiza' and Infobox, neither cited.

fix.text: House is electronic dance music built on a steady kick drum on every beat, usually at about 120–130 beats per minute. It grew in Chicago in the early-to-mid 1980s, when DJs from the city's queer Black underground clubs began reworking disco records to give them a more mechanical beat; the steady kick may have come from DJs adding drum machines under the records they played. From there it spread to New York, London and Ibiza and became a worldwide sound.
